extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; advanced students and scientists interested in the nature of scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explaining criteria and characteristics by which scientific revolutions, paradigms, and their effects on practice, data, and pedagogy can be identified and evaluated. Focuses on how paradigms shape observation, experiment, concepts, textbooks, and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations may remain the same while their paradigm-role changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Postrevolutionary science invariably includes many of the same manipulations, performed with the same instruments and described in the same terms, as its prerevolutionary predecessor; if these enduring manipulations have been changed at all, the change must lie either in their relation to the paradigm or in their concrete results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Dalton: the same chemical operations become indices of different aspects of nature’s regularity when attached to a new paradigm; occasionally identical manipulations yield different concrete results after a paradigm shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms define classificatory criteria (e.g., mixture vs compound)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paradigm in use determines how practitioners distinguish phenomena (for eighteenth-century chemists, affinity theory drew the line separating physical mixtures from chemical compounds in ways unfamiliar after Dalton).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational tests available at the time were insufficient; chemists sought criteria that made solutions compounds because that fit their paradigm. Thus what counts as 'chemical' vs 'physical' is paradigm-dependent (example: Proust vs Berthollet debate on fixed proportions).

rubrics_metrics.name: A paradigm determines which regularities are seen and generalized
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularities (laws) that become salient depend on the paradigm; without abandoning affinity theory and reconceptualizing the domain, generalizations like the law of fixed proportions could not be formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even well-known experimental regularities (e.g., Richter's work) remained recipes until a paradigm allowed their generalization; paradigms enable the re-expression of old data in new forms (e.g., Dalton's weights revealing simple ratios).

rubrics_metrics.name: New paradigms can make certain laws constitutive or tautological
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a new paradigm is accepted its principles can become constitutive, so that a law (e.g., Dalton's law of constant proportions) is no longer something experiment alone could have established beforehand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Dalton, assuming atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios made the law of constant proportion a tautology; acceptance transforms the status of some regularities into principles of the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm adoption leads to new experiments and re-expression of old data
rubrics_metrics.description: A new paradigm suggests new experiments and changes how previous manipulations are recorded and interpreted, making previously unnoticed ratios or regularities jump out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dalton’s paradigm suggested experiments (Gay-Lussac on combining volumes) and changed the recording of data (writing combining weights in atomic ratios), which revealed multiple and fixed proportions previously unrecognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm change can alter even numerical data through shifts in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: As practitioners adopt a new paradigm they 'beat nature into line'; measurements and reported numerical composition can shift as experimental practice and interpretation change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical measurements (e.g., Proust's oxygen ratios) changed over time; the data themselves may be different after a revolution because of changed questions, methods, and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbooks and related literature obscure the existence and role of revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbooks, popularizations, and philosophical works typically address an already articulated body of problems and therefore record the stable outcome of past revolutions, disguising how those outcomes were first recognized and embraced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because textbooks must communicate the vocabulary and syntax of contemporary scientific language, they truncate history, select and distort past work to fit current paradigms, and thereby make revolutions nearly invisible to students and most practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogic presentation produces a misleading image of linear, cumulative development
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbook arrangement—treating experiments, concepts, laws, and theories seriatim—implies science progressed by piecemeal additions toward present paradigms, a portrayal at odds with how science actually develops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'bricks-to-building' image ignores that many contemporary puzzles arose only after recent revolutions and that earlier work pursued different problems with different canons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific concepts gain full meaning only within paradigm-linked context
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal definitions (e.g., of 'element') have little scientific content alone; concepts gain significance only when related to other concepts, manipulative procedures, and paradigm applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle’s 'definition' of element is pedagogic and paraphrastic; the modern chemical concept of element acquired its function through successive revolutions (Boyle, Lavoisier, etc.) and associated practices rather than by a single verbal invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science is puzzle-solving within a paradigm, not testing the paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Research workers engaged in normal science solve puzzles presupposing the paradigm; trial attempts in this mode test approaches, not the paradigm’s rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradigm-testing occurs only after persistent failure leading to crisis and only when an alternate candidate paradigm emerges; analogy: chess problem-solving tries moves within given rules, not the rules themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing and verification of theories is inherently comparative and paradigm-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing a paradigm occurs as part of competition between rival paradigms for the community’s allegiance; verification involves comparing theories' ability to explain actual evidence, but theories and observations are tied to existing paradigms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probabilistic verification schemes that require constructing all alternate theories or all conceivable tests implicitly rely on a neutral observation language; since none exists, such constructions are restricted to paradigm-based traditions and thus disguise the true verification situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful proponents of new paradigms tend to be concentrated on crisis problems and less committed to old paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: New interpretations first arise in a few individuals whose attention intensely concentrates on crisis-provoking problems and who are often young or new enough to be less committed to the old world view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their relative freedom from entrenched practice helps them reorient the field; conversion of the profession requires that these individuals make the transition comprehensible and attractive to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutions reformulate both questions and answers, creating new facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories and the facts they 'fit' emerge together from revolutionary reformulation; some questions could not be asked (or answered) before the new paradigm reframed the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Galileo’s kinematic statements take a different form embedded in Newtonian dynamics; many facts presented in textbooks are outcomes of such reformulations rather than independent empirical discoveries.
